messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric energy harvester (sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{leak}$).
    *   Output: $V_{out}$ to a load $R_L$ and storage capacitor $C_{out}$.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8 \text{V}$ (min)
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6 \text{V}$ (max)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4 \text{s}$ (startup)
        *   $dV \le 0.02 \text{V}$ (stability)
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6): Varying $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, $R_L$.
    *   Critical Observations:
        *   Open-circuit voltage is low ($\sim 3.2 \text{V}$), so diode drops (0.25V for DSCH) are significant.
        *   Reference FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) failed:
            *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{avg}$ too low (1.76V).
            *   S3 (strong excitation, light load): $V_{max}$ too high (5.72V), ripple too high, $dV$ too high.
            *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{avg}$ too low (1.51V), $t_{up}$ too slow.
            *   S5 (low frequency): $dV$ too high.

    *   *Problem 1: Voltage Drop.* Passive rectification (FBR) has two diode drops. At low excitation (S4), this is lethal.
    *   *Problem 2: Overvoltage.* In S3, the voltage climbs above 3.6V because the load is light and excitation is strong. A Zener clamp (DZ33) is needed.
    *   *Problem 3: Efficiency/Cold Start.* To improve $V_{avg}$ and $t_{up}$, especially for weak excitation, we need to minimize drops or use a synchronous technique.
    *   *SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* This is the standard for piezo energy harvesting. It flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the harvested energy.
    *   *Topology for SSHI:*
        *   Usually consists of an inductor $L$ and switches that close at voltage extrema.
        *   A standard SSHI implementation often involves a rectifier (half or full) and a switching circuit.
        *   Since the goal is simplicity and meeting constraints, let's try:
            1.  Synchronous Rectification (via switches) or a modified SSHI.
            2.  Zener clamp to prevent overvoltage (S3).
            3.  Larger storage capacitor to reduce ripple and stability issues.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI-like with Zener Clamp**
        *   Piezo is connected to a rectifier (full bridge or half bridge).
        *   An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ provide the inversion.
        *   Wait, a simpler approach for low-voltage piezo: Parallel SSHI or a basic buck-boost style.
        *   Actually, let's try a **Standard SSHI** (Half-bridge rectifier + SSHI switch).
        *   Wait, let's look at the constraints again. $V_{max} = 3.6\text{V}$. A DZ33 (3.3V Zener) is perfect.

    *   **Design 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge)**
        *   Use switches instead of diodes to eliminate the $V_f$ drop.
        *   Given the "SYNC" controller closes for "ton" and triggers at extrema, it's not a standard PWM controller but a peak-trigger.
        *   If we use `edges: "both"` and a small `ton`, we can implement a charge pump or an SSHI inverter.

    *   **Design 3: FBR + Zener + Larger C (Baseline Improvement)**
        *   The reference FBR failed S2, S3, S4, S5.
        *   S3 (max voltage) $\rightarrow$ Add DZ33.
        *   S2, S4 (min voltage) $\rightarrow$ FBR is too inefficient.
        *   Wait, SSHI is the way to go. Let's refine the SSHI topology.

    *   *Basic SSHI (Inductor-based inversion):*
        *   Piezo $pzp, pzn$.
        *   $C_p$ is internal.
        *   Inductor $L$ is switched across $pzp, pzn$ at the peaks.
        *   Rectifier (e.g., a diode from $pzp$ to $out$ and $pzn$ to $out$ with ground returns) extracts the energy.
        *   Actually, a simpler SSHI:
            - Inductor $L$ between $pzp$ and $n1$.
            - Switch $S1$ between $n1$ and $pzn$.
            - Diode $D1$ from $pzp$ to $out$.
            - Diode $D2$ from $pzn$ to $out$ (Wait, this is a half-bridge).
            - Better: Full bridge rectifier to $out$, plus $L$ and $S$ across the piezo.

    *   *Refined SSHI Topology:*
        1.  Full bridge rectifier (DSCH) from $pzp, pzn$ to $out$.
        2.  Zener clamp (DZ33) from $out$ to $0$.
        3.  Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo ($pzp$ to $pzn$ via $L$ and $S$) to flip the voltage.
        4.  Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ on $out$.

    *   Wait, the SYNC controller triggers at "piezo voltage extrema" (zero crossings of current).
    *   If $S$ closes at extrema, it shorts $pzp$ and $pzn$ through $L$. This is the classic SSHI inversion.
    *   $L$ should be such that $\pi \sqrt{L C_p} \approx t_{on}$.
    *   For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $L = 10\text{mH} \rightarrow t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Proposed Circuit 1: SSHI-FBR*
        *   D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        *   D2: pzn -> out (DSCH) - Wait, this isn't a bridge.
        *   Bridge:
            - D1: pzp -> out
            - D2: pzn -> out (Wait, for a full bridge, the bottom diodes go to ground).
            - D1: pzp -> out
            - D2: pzn -> out
            - D3: 0 -> pzp
            - D4: 0 -> pzn
            - No, that's not right.
            - Correct Full Bridge:
                - D1: pzp -> out
                - D2: pzn -> out
                - D3: 0 -> pzp (Wait, the prompt says "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have their anode on ground)")
                - Let's follow the prompt:
                    D1: ["pzp", "out"]
                    D2: ["pzn", "out"]
                    D3: ["0", "pzp"]
                    D4: ["0", "pzn"]
        *   SSHI Part:
            - L1: ["pzp", "n1"]
            - S1: ["n1", "pzn"]
            - G1: SYNC (edges: "both", phase: 0)
        *   Clamp:
            - D5: ["0", "out"] (DZ33)
        *   Storage:
            - C1: ["out", "0"]

    *   *Proposed Circuit 2: SSHI-Half-Bridge (Simpler, less drop)*
        *   D1: ["pzp", "out"] (DSCH)
        *   L1: ["pzp", "n1"]
        *   S1: ["n1", "pzn"]
        *   G1: SYNC (edges: "both")
        *   C1: ["out", "0"]
        *   D5: ["0", "out"] (DZ33)
        *   Wait, a half-bridge only captures half the cycles. SSHI improves it, but maybe FBR is safer. Let's try SSHI-FBR.

    *   *Proposed Circuit 3: Synchronous Rectification (Ideal Bridge)*
        *   Instead of diodes, use switches.
        *   Wait, I only have 4 switches. A full bridge needs 4.
        *   S1: ["pzp", "out"], S2: ["pzn", "out"], S3: ["0", "pzp"], S4: ["0", "pzn"].
        *   This is too complex to control with only 2 SYNCs.
        *   Let's try a Charge Pump or a simple Switch-Capacitor converter? No, the current is too low.

    *   *Wait, look at S4 (Weak excitation):* $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 1\text{M}\Omega$.
        $V_{oc} = \frac{30\mu\text{A}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 1.91\text{V}$.
        With FBR, we lose $2 \cdot 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$, so $V_{out} \approx 1.41\text{V}$. This explains why FBR failed S4 ($V_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$).
        SSHI increases the voltage. In an ideal SSHI, the voltage across $C_p$ can reach $V_{out} + V_{peak}$.

    *   *Refining the SSHI-FBR:*
        $C_p$ is internal. The SSHI inversion happens *across* the piezo.
        The circuit:
        - D1: pzp -> out
        - D2: pzn -> out
        - D3: 0 -> pzp
        - D4: 0 -> pzn
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn
        - G1: SYNC, edges: "both", ton: 50us
        - C1: out -> 0
        - D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)

    *   *Wait, is there a more efficient way?*
        What if we use a half-bridge with a larger storage capacitor and SSHI?
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: 0 -> pzn (Wait, no)
        Actually, the SSHI inversion $L-S$ already helps a lot. Let's try the SSHI-FBR first.

    *   *One more thought:* A Zener clamp is necessary for S3. But a Zener also adds a small leakage. 3.3V should be fine.

    *   *Wait, check the "S5" failure (dv too high):* This means the voltage is drifting. A larger storage capacitor $C_{out}$ or a better balance of power is needed. $C_{out}$ is optimized automatically, so the topology must allow for stability.

    *   *Checking Component Count:*
        D1, D2, D3, D4 (Bridge) = 4
        L1, S1 (SSHI) = 2
        G1 (SYNC) = 1
        C1 (Storage) = 1
        D5 (Zener) = 1
        Total = 9 components. Well within the 16-component limit.

    *   Let's consider a second topology: **Parallel SSHI (P-SSHI)**.
        In P-SSHI, the inductor is not in series with the piezo but is switched to flip the voltage of a separate capacitor or the piezo itself.
        Actually, the simplest "active" improvement over FBR is just adding the L-S inversion.

    *   Let's consider a third topology: **Half-Bridge SSHI**.
        Some papers suggest a half-bridge is more efficient if the inversion is strong.
        D1: pzp -> out
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn
        G1: SYNC
        C1: out -> 0
        D5: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        But FBR is more robust.

    *   Let's try:
        1. SSHI-FBR (Full Bridge + Inversion + Clamp)
        2. SSHI-HalfBridge (Half Bridge + Inversion + Clamp)
        3. FBR + Clamp (Just to see if the Zener alone fixes S3 and if the optimizer can fix others, though unlikely). Actually, let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" style if possible.

    *   *Wait, SYNC controller detail:*
        "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds at the piezo voltage extrema".
        This is perfect for SSHI.

    *   *Let's double-check the Full Bridge again:*
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        If $pzp$ is positive, D1 conducts. If $pzn$ is positive, D2 conducts.
        If $pzp$ is negative, D3 conducts. If $pzn$ is negative, D4 conducts.
        Wait, if $pzp$ is positive, $pzn$ is usually negative.
        So:
        Cycle 1: $pzp > 0, pzn < 0 \rightarrow$ D1 and D4 conduct.
        Cycle 2: $pzp < 0, pzn > 0 \rightarrow$ D2 and D3 conduct.
        This is a standard full bridge.

    *   *Final Polish for Design 1 (SSHI-FBR):*
        D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
        D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
        D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
        D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
        L1: pzp, n1 (10mH)
        S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
        G1: SYNC (ton: 50us, edges: "both", phase: 0)
        C1: out, 0 (2.2uF)
        D5: 0, out (DZ33)

    *   *Design 2 (SSHI-Half):*
        D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
        L1: pzp, n1 (10mH)
        S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
        G1: SYNC (ton: 50us, edges: "both", phase: 0)
        C1: out, 0 (2.2uF)
        D5: 0, out (DZ33)
        Wait, a half-bridge only collects current when $pzp > V_{out}$. With SSHI, we can potentially collect more. But let's stick to the full bridge as the primary.

    *   *Design 3 (Alternative Active Rectification):*
        Maybe a "Synchronous Bridge" using the switches?
        If we have only 2 SYNCs, we could do:
        S1: pzp, out (G1)
        S2: pzn, out (G2)
        S3: 0, pzp (G1)
        S4: 0, pzn (G2)
        G1: SYNC (edges: "pos")
        G2: SYNC (edges: "neg")
        This would be a fully synchronous bridge.
        - When G1 is active (pos peak), S1 and S3 close. $pzp$ is connected to $out$, $0$ is connected to $pzp$. Wait, that shorts $out$ to $0$.
        - Let's re-think:
            S1: pzp, out
            S2: 0, pzn
            G1: SYNC (edges: "pos", ton: some value)
            - This would connect $pzp$ to $out$ and $pzn$ to $0$.
            S3: pzn, out
            S4: 0, pzp
            G2: SYNC (edges: "neg", ton: some value)
            - This would connect $pzn$ to $out$ and $pzp$ to $0$.
        - This is a fully synchronous bridge. No diode drops.
        - For S4, this would be huge.
        - But we still need a Zener clamp for S3.
        - And we need a storage capacitor.
        - Does this replace the SSHI? Yes, it's a different approach (Synchronous Rectification vs. SSHI).

    *   *Wait, let's refine the Synchronous Bridge:*
        S1: pzp, out, ctrl: G1
        S2: pzn, 0, ctrl: G1
        S3: pzn, out, ctrl: G2
        S4: pzp, 0, ctrl: G2
        G1: SYNC, edges: "pos", ton: 1ms (Wait, ton is max 0.001s = 1ms. But we want it to stay closed for the whole half-cycle. The SYNC controller only closes for "ton". This is a problem. The SYNC controller is for *pulses* at the extrema, not for the whole half-period.)
        - Re-reading: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
        - This means the SYNC controller *cannot* be used for continuous rectification. It's specifically designed for SSHI (short pulses at peaks).

    *   *Conclusion:* I must use diodes for the rectification part and SYNC for the SSHI inversion.

    *   *Wait, I can use a "Switch-Capacitor" style or just stick with SSHI.*
        Let's go with:
        1. SSHI-FBR (Full Bridge + Inversion + Clamp)
        2. SSHI-HalfBridge (Half Bridge + Inversion + Clamp) - Just in case.
        3. FBR-Clamp (Full Bridge + Clamp) - To see if the optimizer can fix the FBR by just adding the Zener and adjusting C.

    *   *Wait, one more SSHI variant:* The inductor can be on the output side, but that's more complex. Let's stick to the standard one.

    *   *Final check on SSHI-FBR components:*
        D1, D2, D3, D4: Bridge
        D5: Zener clamp
        C1: Storage cap
        L1: Inversion inductor
        S1: Inversion switch
        G1: SYNC controller
        (Total: 9 components)

    *   *Let's think about the ton for G1 again.*
        $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        For $L=10\text{mH}$, $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $t_{on} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
        The optimizer will tune $L$ and $t_{on}$, so I'll provide reasonable starting values.

    *   *Wait, the Zener clamp:*
        S3 has $V_{max} = 5.72\text{V}$ with FBR. A 3.3V Zener will definitely clip this. But will it clip too much?
        The limit is 3.6V. 3.3V is fine.

    *   *Is the SSHI too much?*
        If $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$, and we add SSHI, the voltage can double.
        $V_{out}$ might hit 3.3V quickly. The Zener will then keep it there.
        This should solve S2 and S4 (by increasing harvested energy) and S3 (by clamping).

    *   *Double check:- "S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C" - FBR failed "settled" (dv > 0.02V).*
        Low frequency means larger ripple and slower charging. A larger $C_{out}$ (optimized) and the SSHI's higher efficiency should help the output settle.

    *   *Correcting the Bridge diodes again:*
        Prompt: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        Wait, if $pzp$ is positive, D1 conducts. If $pzn$ is negative, D4 conducts.
        If $pzp$ is negative, D3 conducts. If $pzn$ is positive, D2 conducts.
        Yes, this is correct.

    *   *Wait, if $pzp$ is positive, and D1 conducts, $V_{out}$ becomes $V_{pzp} - V_f$.*
    *   *If $pzp$ is negative, and D3 conducts, $V_{pzp}$ is clamped to $-V_f$ relative to ground.*
    *   *This is a correct full bridge.*

    *   *One last thing: The SYNC phase.*
        For SSHI, the switch should close at the peak of the voltage, which is the zero crossing of the current. The prompt says: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current."
        This means `phase: 0` is already at the extrema.

    *   *Final check on the proposals:*
        Proposal 1: SSHI-FBR (FBR + L-S Inversion + Zener)
        Proposal 2: SSHI-Half (Half-bridge + L-S Inversion + Zener)
        Proposal 3: FBR-Clamp (FBR + Zener)

    *   *Let's reconsider Proposal 2:* A half-bridge is just:
        D1: pzp -> out
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn
        G1: SYNC
        C1: out -> 0
        D5: 0 -> out
        Actually, this only collects during the positive half-cycle. SSHI will flip the negative half-cycle voltage to positive, but you still need a way to get it to $out$.
        If the inversion is $V_{pzp} \rightarrow -V_{pzp}$, then:
        Pos half-cycle: $pzp$ is positive $\rightarrow$ D1 conducts.
        Neg half-cycle: $pzp$ is negative $\rightarrow$ L-S flips it to positive $\rightarrow$ D1 conducts.
        So a half-bridge *can* work with SSHI. It's more efficient (one diode drop instead of two).
        Let's use that as Proposal 2.
